questions.q: Which statement most precisely describes a classical bit at any given instant?
options: It is a physical system in exactly one of two definite states, with any uncertainty belonging to the observer, not the bit
It is a physical system that can be in both of its two states at once with some probability of each
It is a purely mathematical label that has no physical implementation
It is a system that holds a continuous value between 0 and 1 until it is rounded at readout
questions.explain: A classical bit is always in one definite physical state (a voltage level, a magnetic domain orientation, etc.). If you don't know which state it's in, that reflects your lack of information, not the bit's actual physical condition — it is never genuinely 'undecided.' This determinism is exactly what quantum states will not preserve.

questions.q: A system of n classical bits has 2^n possible configurations. What does this number actually describe?
options: The number of configurations the system could be in across different inputs or times — at any single instant the system is in exactly one of them
The number of distinct states the system occupies simultaneously at every instant
The number of bits required to store one configuration
The maximum number of operations the system can perform per second
questions.explain: 2^n counts the size of the possibility space, not how many states are realized at once. An 8-bit register has 256 possible byte values, but at any given moment it holds exactly one of them — say 01101010 — never a blend of several. Confusing 'size of the possibility space' with 'number of simultaneously occupied states' is the single most common error when people later try to describe superposition.

questions.q: Which of the following is a genuinely special property of classical bits that this lesson identifies as something quantum states will NOT share?
options: You can read or copy a classical bit's value without disturbing or altering the original
A classical bit can be labeled 0 or 1 depending on convention
A classical bit is implemented using some physical medium, such as a voltage or magnetic domain
A system of classical bits can represent more than one value across its lifetime
questions.explain: Non-disturbing readout and copying is easy to take for granted with classical information — reading a cached value or duplicating a file doesn't change the original. This property fails for quantum states (formalized later as the no-cloning theorem) and is one of the sharpest breaks between classical and quantum information.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call classical information a 'strictly weaker' model, rather than just a simpler one?
options: Because the classical model has no mechanism for a single system to carry structured information about multiple possibilities at once in a way that can later interfere before measurement
Because classical bits require more physical hardware per bit of storage than quantum bits
Because classical computers run at slower clock speeds than quantum computers in all cases
Because classical bits cannot be organized into registers larger than a few dozen bits
questions.explain: The limitation isn't about speed or hardware cost — it's structural. Classical bits are always in one definite state, with any uncertainty being purely about the observer's knowledge (epistemic probability). There is no classical mechanism for amplitude-like interference, where possibilities can reinforce or cancel each other before you look. Quantum mechanics adds exactly that extra structure, which is why it isn't just 'more bits, faster.'

questions.q: A friend says, 'An unread classical bit in memory is like a coin that's both heads and tails until you look at it.' Based on this lesson's definition, what is wrong with that analogy?
options: The bit is always in one definite physical state the whole time; 'both heads and tails' describes the observer's uncertainty, not the bit's actual physical condition
Nothing is wrong — this is exactly how a classical bit behaves
The analogy is wrong only because coins are three-dimensional and bits are not
The analogy is wrong because classical bits cannot be read at all, even once
questions.explain: This is the determinism property: the bit's physical state is fixed and singular at every instant, whether or not anyone has checked it. 'Both heads and tails' is a classical-probability way of talking about the friend's own ignorance, not a true physical description of the bit itself. This distinction is exactly what makes real quantum superposition (covered next lesson) a different and stranger claim than 'secretly both.'
